This module sits beside the solver. No other remlax module imports it, and it
modifies none of them. It consumes the output of `fit_reml`.

| file | role |
|---|---|
| `inst/python/remlax/scan.py` | the algebra: projection, covariate families, tests. Pure NumPy, no JAX required |
| `inst/python/remlax/scan_cli.py` | entry point, run by `inst/python/remlax_run.py scan_cli`, beside `cli.py` |
| `R/scan.R` | `rx_scan()` / `rx_scan_threshold()` |
| `R/scan_loco.R` | `rx_scan_loco()` / `rx_scan_exact()`, built on `rx_scan()` |
| `tests-python/test_scan.py` | the scan checked against the Wald test with the column added to X |
| `validation/etude_scan_familles.py` (remlax-validation) | which covariate detects which mechanism |

---

## 1. Principle

The scan is an EMMAX-type GWAS (Kang et al. 2010). Variance components are
estimated once under the null hypothesis. Each SNP is then tested as a fixed
effect at fixed V. For a column `s` added to `X`,

```
beta_s = (s'Ps)^-1 s'Py      var(beta_s) = (s'Ps)^-1      chi2 = (s'Py)^2/(s'Ps)
P = V^-1 - V^-1 X (X'V^-1 X)^-1 X'V^-1
```

This formula is the one in `fixed_tests.wald`, rewritten for one column. Since V
does not change, the score and Wald tests coincide.

### Covariance structures beyond diagonalisation

`gaston` and `statgenGWAS` speed up the scan by diagonalising
`V = sigma_g^2 K + sigma_e^2 I`. This shortcut requires a single kernel and an
iid residual. With two kernels (direct and indirect), an AR1 residual or
heterogeneous residual sections, V no longer diagonalises. `remlax.scan` does
not need to diagonalise, so it accepts any V that the solver can assemble.

### Projection at the genotype level

The marker covariates are defined at the genotype level, where q is of the
order of a few hundred. P is projected once onto the design incidences, with
`c_f = Z_f' P y` and `C_fg = Z_f' P Z_g`. The p statistics then follow from
matrix products in dimension q:

```
num_f(j)  = m_j' c_f            den_fg(j) = m_j' C_fg m_j
```

The cost drops from O(n^2 p) to O(q^2 p). Moreover, the projection requires no
new factorisation. `fit_reml` already returns `Vi`, `vbeta` and `Py`, so
`C_fg = Z_f' Vi Z_g - (Z_f' Vi X) vbeta (X' Vi Z_g)`.

---

## 2. Covariate families

Let `m_j` denote the doses of SNP j. `Z_dir` is the incidence of the genotype
carried by the plant. `Z_ind` is the weighted incidence of the genotypes of its
neighbours.

| family | covariate | interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `dir` | `Z_dir m` | direct genetic effect, the standard GWAS |
| `ind` | `Z_ind m` | indirect genetic effect: allelic dose of the neighbour |
| `sim` | `(Z_dir m) * (Z_ind m)` | focal x neighbour allelic similarity |

`sim` is the covariate of Sato et al. (2021, 2024). Under +/-1 coding, the
product equals +1 when the neighbour carries the same allele and -1 otherwise.
It is also exactly the interaction term between the direct effect and the
neighbour effect. This term is a DGE x IGE interaction.

### The published models are not nested

Sato's model contains `dir` and `sim`, never `ind`. The indirect genetic effect
model of Muir (2005) and Bijma (2011) contains `dir` and `ind`, never `sim`.
Each model expresses a distinct biological hypothesis, and neither is a
reparametrisation of the other.

- `ind`: a neighbour carrying allele A depresses the focal plant, whatever the
  genotype of the focal plant. This is a dose effect.
- `sim`: the effect depends on allelic concordance. This is a frequency effect.
  Sato links it to overyielding in mixtures (2024, 2026).

`sim` requires centred doses (+/-1 coding). Under 0/1/2 coding, the product is
not a similarity. `scan()` then rejects the family. Otherwise it would return a
wrong result with nothing to flag it.

---

## 3. Test specifications

The bar denotes a conditional test of the term given the others, as in asreml
and in `fixed_tests.wald`.

| specification | df | effect tested |
|---|---|---|
| `dir` | 1 | standard GWAS |
| `ind` | 1 | additive neighbour effect, alone |
| `sim` | 1 | similarity, alone |
| `dir+sim` | 2 | Sato's model |
| `dir+ind` | 2 | the additive IGE model |
| `dir+ind+sim` | 3 | all families jointly |
| `ind\|dir+sim` | 1 | additive neighbour effect in addition to Sato's model |
| `sim\|dir+ind` | 1 | interaction in addition to the additive effects |

The last two rows are tests that existed nowhere before. They discriminate
between the two readings.

---

## 4. Covariates and the mechanisms they detect

The study is in `validation/etude_scan_familles.py`, in the remlax-validation repository. It uses a randomised
block design with n = 360 observations, q = 90 genotypes, p = 300 SNPs and 300
replicates. Its polygenic background is direct + indirect with a covariance
(`us` 2x2), and the residual is AR1 within blocks. The null model of the scan
is the true model. A single causal SNP carries a varying mechanism. Its
contribution is calibrated on the variance scale, with a standard deviation of
0.40. The covariates differ in dispersion, so equal coefficients would compare
signals of different amplitude.

Detection rate of the causal SNP at the Bonferroni threshold, in %:

| tested model | lambda | direct effect | neighbour allele | similarity | both |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dir` | 1.03 | 30 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `ind` | 1.02 | 0 | 97 | 0 | 53 |
| `sim` | 0.99 | 0 | 0 | 99 | 74 |
| `dir+sim` (Sato) | 1.01 | 21 | 0 | 98 | 62 |
| `dir+ind` (additive IGE) | 1.01 | 22 | 94 | 0 | 44 |
| `dir+ind+sim` | 1.00 | 18 | 91 | 97 | 95 |
| `ind\|dir+sim` | 1.01 | 0 | 96 | 0 | 54 |
| `sim\|dir+ind` | 0.99 | 0 | 0 | 99 | 73 |

All tests are calibrated (lambda from 0.99 to 1.03), so their powers are
comparable.

### Reading the table

Neither published model detects the mechanism of the other. The blindness is
total, at 0 % in both cases. Sato's product term does not approximate an
additive neighbourhood effect, and the converse holds too. Under randomisation,
the neighbour dose and the focal x neighbour product are practically
orthogonal.

The conditional tests separate the mechanisms directly. `ind|dir+sim` detects
the additive neighbour effect in 96 % of cases and never fires on pure
similarity. `sim|dir+ind` behaves in exactly the symmetric way. These two tests
are the ones to run when the operating mechanism is unknown. In practice, it is
never known in advance.

The model with all three families is the only one robust to a mixture of
mechanisms. In the realistic case, both mechanisms operate together. This model
then reaches 95 %, against 62 % for Sato's model and 44 % for the additive
model. The extra degrees of freedom cost power when a single mechanism
operates. Against the test of that family alone, the three-family model loses
6 points on the neighbour allele (91 % against 97 %), 2 points on similarity
(97 % against 99 %) and 12 points on the direct effect (18 % against 30 %).

### Scope of the table

The table does not address the specification of the variance components. Its
simulated polygenic background is direct + indirect, without a similarity
kernel, and the null matches it. The design note treats a separate issue. A
null that omits the component matching the tested covariate produces false
positives (lambda 1.48). An iid residual does too when the truth is AR1
(lambda 1.12).

---

## 5. External validation

Validation runs `validation/etude_scan_vs_rrblup.R`, then `.py`, in the remlax-validation repository. The scan
accepts V matrices that GWAS packages cannot handle. No external reference
therefore exists for the case of interest. A reference exists for the
degenerate case of the EMMAX model, where the two should coincide. This model
has a single kernel, an iid residual and one observation per genotype.
`rrBLUP::GWAS(P3D = TRUE)` serves as the reference. It is pure R and therefore
loads everywhere. The neighbouring script `etude_scan_vs_statgen.R` does the
same with statgenGWAS, for users who can load it. Variance components estimated
by rrBLUP are imposed on the scan. This setup checks the scan algebra.
Component estimation is tested elsewhere.

The two methods test slightly different statistics, and the difference can be
reconstructed exactly. rrBLUP re-estimates the residual scale at each SNP, on
the residuals of the model that contains the SNP, and reports an F(1, n−2).
The scan keeps the scale of the null model and reports a chi2 with 1 df. Their
relation is exact and requires nothing new in dimension n:

```
Fstat_j = chi2_j * v2 / (y'Py - num_j^2/den_j)        v2 = n - 2
```

`num_j` and `den_j` are columns of the scan output. `y'Py` is a scalar computed
once. These raw quantities are kept for precisely this reason (§8).

On q = 250 genotypes and p = 800 SNPs, the rrBLUP score reconstructed in this
way matches the score rrBLUP reports. Its maximum discrepancy is 3.2·10⁻¹¹ over
the 800 SNPs. No algebraic disagreement remains. Both implementations solve the
same GLS, and the difference in convention is fully explained.

### Cost of the fixed-V convention

The data set is the same, with one causal SNP of large effect.

| | chi2 at fixed V | rrBLUP F | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| causal SNP | 9.778 | 10.554 | −0.776 |
| null SNPs (median) | | | +0.0007 |
| null SNPs (5–95 % quantiles) | | | [−0.0011, +0.0014] |

Values are in −log₁₀(p). On null SNPs, the two conventions are
indistinguishable. Error control and lambda are unaffected. On a SNP of large
effect, the fixed-V test loses 0.78 units of −log₁₀(p). This loss amounts to a
factor of about 6 on the p-value. The measurement quantifies the
conservativeness described in §9. It leaves calibration intact and costs some
significance at the top of the list. This result also gives an order of magnitude to the
case for exact refitting of the top hits.

---

## 6. Measured cost

On 20 cores, in double precision, at the dimensions of the IGE project
(n = 16,211 observations, q = 286 genotypes, 8 fixed effects):

| step | measured at p = 2,000 | extrapolated to p = 127,562 |
|---|---|---|
| projection (once, independent of p) | 1.59 s | 1.59 s |
| scan `dir`, `ind`, `dir+ind` | 0.06 s | 3.6 s |
| scan `dir+ind+sim` | 5.08 s | 324 s |

The `sim` step is a product `Vi @ S3` over blocks of SNPs, measured at
207 GFLOPS fp64. At full size it amounts to 6.7·10^13 operations. This step is
the only one in dimension n in the module. Its cost is linear in p, hence the
extrapolation. On GPU it is an ordinary GEMM. Passing `xp=jax.numpy` to
`scan()` substitutes the device without changing anything else.

Linear families are thus free compared with the null fit. The bilinear
family costs a few minutes of CPU time. This question was left open in the
design note. It is now settled, and favourably.

---

## 7. Usage

### From R

The scan runs on a model that has already been fitted. Nothing is refitted.
The estimated theta is read back and only evaluated.

```r
library(remlax)

fit  <- rx_fit(model)                        # the usual fit
gwas <- rx_scan(fit, model,
                markers    = M,              # q x p, GENOTYPE-level doses in +/-1
                map        = map,            # snp, chr, pos
                incidences = c(dir = "gen", ind = "voisin"),
                tests      = c("dir", "ind", "dir+ind+sim",
                               "ind|dir+sim", "sim|dir+ind"),
                maf = 0.05)
attr(gwas, "meta")$lambda_gc                 # genomic control per test
rx_scan_threshold(gwas, "ind|dir+sim")       # Bonferroni over the tested SNPs
```

`incidences` names the model terms that carry `Z_dir` and `Z_ind`. It takes
term names and no matrices. By construction, the scan therefore uses the design
of the null model. A scan run on an incidence different from that of the fit
would be a silent error. The interface prevents it.

### Evaluation without refitting

Estimation needs no refit, but one evaluation of the model is required. The
variance components are not re-estimated. `rx_scan` writes the theta of `fit` back into the bundle and
runs the solver with `--theta-in --maxiter 0`. `fit_reml` explicitly
short-circuits this case (message "evaluation only (maxiter = 0), no optimisation",
`n_iter = 0`).

However, `Vi`, `vbeta` and `Py` are n x n objects that live in the fitting
process and are never written to disk. At n = 16,000, `Vi` weighs 2 GB. V must
therefore be reassembled once and factorised. This step evaluates the objective
once and performs no optimisation.

Measured on a design with n = 480, q = 120, two kernels and p = 400 SNPs:

| | time | |
|---|---|---|
| full fit (`rx_fit`) | 12.84 s | 10 iterations |
| `rx_scan` end to end, seen from R | 12.78 s | bundle export, process launch, JAX import, compilation, evaluation, inverse, scan |
| of which the solver's "null model" step | 8.98 s | `n_iter = 0` |
| of which projection | 0.006 s | |
| of which scan of 400 SNPs, 4 tests | 0.252 s | |

The decisive check is the likelihood. Re-evaluated `-2logL` equals 1651.222759,
against 1651.2228 at the fit, with a difference of 0.000e+00. Theta and the
likelihood are identical to the bit. Nothing was therefore re-estimated.

On the same model, the solver logs separately `[compilation] 4,0 s | une
evaluation : 0,015 s`. For sizing purposes, one evaluation costs 15 ms. The
rest of the 12.78 s is start-up. It consists of process launch, JAX import,
compilation, bundle writing and the explicit inverse. None of these steps is
optimisation, and none grows with p. A step-by-step breakdown of the 12.78 s
was not instrumented. Only the three rows of the table are timed separately.

In practice, `rx_scan` needs only the theta of a fitted model to scan it. The
pipeline writes theta to `theta_06v.npy`. This file is currently declared
outside the contract. If the pipeline keeps theta, a scan can start without
touching the fit.

### One null per chromosome and exact refit of the top hits

`rx_scan()` uses one null model whose relationship matrix contains the tested
SNP and its neighbours in linkage disequilibrium. The polygenic term then
absorbs part of the effect of the SNP. `rx_scan_loco()` fits one null per
chromosome, with the relationship matrix computed without that chromosome
(leave one chromosome out), and scans the chromosome under this null.

At fixed V, a SNP of large effect is tested under an overestimated residual
variance (§5). `rx_scan_exact()` refits the model for the top SNPs, with the
SNP as a fixed effect, and returns a Wald test with re-estimated variance
components. A REML likelihood ratio test cannot be used here: two models with
different fixed effects do not share the same restricted likelihood.

Both functions receive the model as a function, `build(K, X_sup = NULL)`.
It returns the `rx_model` for a relationship matrix `K` and, when given, extra
fixed-effect columns `X_sup`. The relationship matrix can then change without
guessing where it enters the model, and the design of the null is kept by
construction. `K_of(W)` computes the relationship matrix from a dose matrix.

```r
build <- function(K, X_sup = NULL) {
  X <- cbind(model.matrix(~ rep, d), X_sup)
  rx_model(d$y, X, list(rx_term("dge_ige", list(Zd, Zn), K = K, struct = "us"),
                        rx_term("bloc", d$bloc)), rx_residual())
}
incid <- c(dir = "dge_ige:1", ind = "dge_ige:2")
loco  <- rx_scan_loco(build, K_of, M, map, incidences = incid,
                      tests = c("dir", "ind", "dir+ind"),
                      fit_args = list(backend = "cpu"))
attr(loco, "loco")                           # one null per chromosome
tetes <- rx_scan_exact(loco, "ind", build, K_of, M, map, incid, top = 8,
                       fit_args = list(backend = "cpu"))
```

The example of `demo/test_gwas_dge_ige.R` (remlax-validation) has 300
genotypes with 4 replicates, 5 chromosomes of 500 SNPs with linkage
disequilibrium and two subpopulations. Polygenic DGE and IGE are correlated,
with one causal SNP of direct effect on chromosome 2 and one of indirect effect
on chromosome 4.

| | fixed V, one null | LOCO | LOCO and exact refit |
|---|---|---|---|
| indirect causal SNP, −log₁₀(p) | 8.02 (rank 1) | 9.23 (rank 1) | 10.2 |
| direct causal SNP, −log₁₀(p) | 3.25 (rank 2) | 3.71 (rank 13) | |
| genomic control lambda, `dir` and `ind` | 0.97 to 0.98 | 1.18 to 1.28 | |
| time on CPU | 13 s | 132 s | |

LOCO and the exact refit both raise the signal of the indirect causal SNP. The
estimated indirect effect goes to 0.370 (standard error 0.057), against a true
value of 0.347. LOCO also raises lambda. The polygenic effects are spread over
all chromosomes in this simulation. A SNP then tags part of the polygenic
signal of its own chromosome, which the LOCO relationship matrix no longer
absorbs. This inflation does not by itself indicate a loss of calibration, but
it was not measured on null simulations.

### Cross-species case

When the neighbours belong to another species, set
`markers = list(dir = M_ble, ind = M_luzerne)`. The scan then tests the
effect of the alleles of the partner on the phenotype of the focal plant. Joint
tests are refused in this case, because column j of the two matrices does not
refer to the same SNP.

### From Python

Inside the fitting process, the functions are called directly:

```python
from remlax.scan import project, scan, lambda_gc
proj = project(fit, X, {"dir": Zdir, "ind": Zind})
r = scan(proj, M, tests=["dir", "ind", "ind|dir+sim"])
lambda_gc(r["chi2_ind|dir+sim"])
```

---

## 8. Outputs

The output holds one vector per SNP. Each requested test produces
`chi2_<test>`, `df_<test>` and `p_<test>`. Tests with 1 df also produce
`beta_<test>` and `se_<test>`. The further columns are listed below.

- `num_<f>`, `den_<f>_<g>`: the raw score quantities. They are kept because
  they allow any contrast to be reconstructed afterwards without rerunning the
  scan.
- `den_ind_ind`: the information available for the indirect effect at this
  SNP. The neighbourhood covariate is an average over J neighbours, so its
  variance collapses for rare alleles. Filter on this quantity as well as on the
  MAF.
- `r_dir_ind`: the correlation between the direct and indirect covariates,
  conditional on V and X. This correlation is the central warning of Sato
  (2021), who diagnoses it by simulation. Here it is obtained as an exact
  by-product. A SNP with `|r|` close to 1 has no separable direct and indirect
  effects. Interpret such a SNP through the joint test only.

---

## 9. Missing features

- A multi-trait scan is not yet available. The formulas are the same with
  N = n t and one 2t x 2t block per SNP. `rx_scan` refuses a term with t > 1 to
  avoid returning a wrong result.
- `rx_scan_exact()` refits the linear tests only (`dir`, `ind`, `dir+ind`).
  The bilinear family `sim` and the conditional tests are not refitted.
- The calibration of `rx_scan_loco()` remains to be measured on null
  simulations. In wheat, it multiplies the number of null fits by 21.
- REML estimation of the neighbourhood range is not yet available. Sato sweeps
  this range over a grid (J = 0, 4, 12). Since the remlax gradient is analytic
  in V, a neighbourhood decay parameter receives its gradient without extra
  code. Its joint identifiability with sigma^2_indirect remains to be checked.
- Permutation tests differ in cost depending on what is permuted. Permuting the
  genomic positions leaves V unchanged. The null fit is then reused at no cost.
  Permuting the neighbourhoods changes Z_ind and the indirect kernel. In that
  case, the null must be refitted at each permutation.
